figures.caption: Fig. 2: Still image of a crowd experiment in which participants were again instructed to imagine being on the way to a concert of their favorite artist [14]. The image shows a typical distribution of behavior and densities: Close to the gate people are pushing and density is high. Density gradually decreases toward the end of the crowds. The participants in the margins of the crowd leave gaps in front of them and some display “unmotivated” behavior.

Fig. 8: Same simulated trajectories as in Figure 7, now colored by each agent’s mean motivation (cividis colormap; darker blue = lower, lighter yellow = higher). The uniform-motivation baseline produces uniform, broadly spread trajectories. The individual terms P , V , and SE each introduce partial differentiation. The combined EV P model yields the most structured pattern, with high-motivation agents converging tightly near the bottleneck.

Fig. 9: Trajectories of participants for two low-motivation runs (nM: 1C060, 2C020) and two high-motivation runs (hM: 2C070, 2C120) from the CROMA experiments [14, 19]. Trajectories show that participants moved from the lower part through the corridor toward the bottleneck. Knots in the trajectories indicate where participants waited for the gate to open. Filled markers show each agent’s position at the moment the door opens; the dashed line at y = 20m marks the door line. The nM runs show wider lateral spread, while the hM runs converge more directly toward the entrance.

Fig. 3: Illustration of the EVP components and the resulting motivation (see Equation (1)). Each subplot shows how spatial expectancy, value, payoff, and their combination into the overall motivation profile depend on distance, agent identity, or normalized rank.

Fig. 4: Rank–area band plots across ten paired seeds. Solid lines are the across-seed median; shaded regions are the interquartile range. The EVP band rises with rank while the base-model band stays flat, consistent with the statistical tests reported in the text (Wilcoxon p = 0.005, Cliff’s δ = 1).

Fig. 10: EVP simulations matched one-to-one to the four CROMA runs in Figure 9. Each panel uses one configuration parameter per condition: the value range [vmin, vmax] is set to [1, 3] for the two nM panels (low intrinsic value, hence low motivation) and to [4, 7] for the two hM panels (high intrinsic value, hence high motivation). All other parameters are identical across panels: EVP motivation mode, closed door (open-time > horizon), N matched to the experiment (85, 87, 89, 87), and the same EVP/payoff parameters as in Table 1. Agents are placed by random distribution in the simulation corridor (not at experimental positions); the comparison is therefore on trajectory shape, not on initial coordinates. Filled markers show each agent’s final position; the dashed line at y = 19m is the simulation door line.

Fig. 5: Rank–area curves from the CROMA experiments grouped by motivation condition. Rank is defined by crossing order at the door; Voronoi area is computed with the same PedPy settings as the simulation. Both groups show a monotone upward trend (ordering structure is universal), but the hM group operates at a distinctly lower absolute area level (stronger overall compression).

Fig. 7: Simulated trajectories (N = 80, closed door, single seed) for each submodel, plotted in a single color for direct visual comparability with the CROMA experimental trajectories in Figure 9. Filled markers indicate each agent’s final position.
